steps.description: Fit the within-subject differential expression model on the raw integer counts. Pre-filter minimally: keep genes with at least 10 counts in at least 5 samples (the smallest group size). Build the DESeqDataSet from the raw counts with no pre-scaling, no gene-length correction and no tximport — featureCounts output is already gene-level integer counts. Run the DESeq2 Wald test; extract results for the contrast (condition, treated, control) so a positive log2 fold change means higher in treated. Adjust with BH, independent filtering on, alpha = 0.05 passed to results() to match the reporting cutoff. Also run the GC-content and gene-length bias diagnostic: for each sample against the median sample, plot the log count ratio against gene GC content and against gene length using a human gene annotation resolved from the reference environment, and report whether a trend exists. plan.title: Paired treated vs control blood RNA-seq DE (n=5 subjects)
plan.analytical_narrative:
The input is a single gene-level raw integer count matrix from STAR/featureCounts (/eval-eight-arms-with-paired-n5-1/data/inputs/counts/counts.csv, 12,000 genes x 10 sample columns plus a gene-symbol first column) and a 10-row sample table (/eval-eight-arms-with-paired-n5-1/data/inputs/metadata/metadata.csv) with subject and condition. Five human blood subjects each contribute one control and one treated sample, so the design is perfectly paired and balanced (5 pairs, 2 conditions). The research question — which genes respond to treatment within each subject — is exactly a within-subject (blocked) two-condition contrast, so the subject enters the design as a fixed blocking term ahead of condition: ~ subject + condition. That removes the between-subject variation from the test, which is the whole point of the paired collection and is the main source of power at n=5.

Step T1S1 runs sample-structure QC before any test: blind VST, PCA on the 500 most variable genes, a sample-distance heatmap, and library sizes, coloured by subject and by condition. With paired data the expected picture is that samples pair by subject on the leading PCs; a swapped or mismatched pair is the failure this step must catch, since a mislabelled pairing silently corrupts the blocked model. T1S2 fits the model: minimal pre-filter (>=10 counts in at least 5 samples, the smallest group size), median-of-ratios size factors estimated inside DESeq2 on the raw counts (no pre-scaling, no length correction, no tximport — the counts are already gene-level from featureCounts), Wald test on the condition coefficient with treated versus control named explicitly, apeglm shrinkage of the reported log2 fold change, BH adjustment at alpha 0.05 with independent filtering, and the p-value histogram inspected before the adjustment. With 5 replicates per cell DESeq2 flags count outliers by Cook's distance and sets those p-values to NA rather than replacing counts, so the number of NA genes from the outlier flag must be reported separately from those the independent filter removed. Because the counts come from an aligner plus a counter with no bias model, the step also runs the GC/length bias diagnostic (log count ratio against the median sample versus gene GC and gene length); cqn and EDASeq are not installed, so if a trend appears the step reports it as a caveat rather than correcting it.

T1S3 is the robustness and reporting step: an edgeR quasi-likelihood F-test on the same counts under the same ~ subject + condition design, the intersection with the DESeq2 calls as the high-confidence set, per-subject paired log-ratio plots for the top genes (which is what makes the within-subject framing concrete rather than assumed), the MA and dispersion diagnostics, and the full reproducibility record. No enrichment step is planned: the question asks which genes respond, not which pathways, and an unasked enrichment would be scope the user did not request. The honest limit to state throughout is n=5 pairs — the pairing buys power but the study still detects only moderate-to-large consistent effects, and a null result for a given gene is not evidence of no response.
